title: The Winter Is Past: Love in Springtime
summary: The woman and the man trade images of flowers and trees, and she describes being brought to the house of wine and resting in his embrace, then charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love until the time is right. Her beloved comes leaping over the hills and calls her to come away with him, because winter is over and spring has come. The chapter ends with a warning about little foxes, a declaration of mutual belonging, and her call for him to return like a gazelle.
story: Chapter 1 opened with the woman's longing and ended with the lovers praising each other. Chapter 2 continues that exchange and then brings the first section of the Song to a close with a refrain (verse 7) that will be repeated twice more in the book (3:5; 8:4). A new scene begins in verse 8: the man arrives and invites her into the springtime. The chapter introduces two of the Song's most important patterns: the charge not to awaken love before its time, and the declaration that the lovers belong to each other. These refrains give the book its shape and much of its meaning.
historical: The chapter's geography is Israel's own. Sharon was the fertile coastal plain between Joppa and Mount Carmel, known for its pastures and wildflowers (Isaiah 35:2). The spring season described in verses 11 to 13 fits the climate of the land: the rains of winter end around March or April, wildflowers cover the hills, fig trees put out their early fruit, and migrating turtledoves return. The mountains of Bether in verse 17 are hard to identify. Bether may be a place name, or the word may mean separation or cleft, describing rugged, divided hills. Since the chapter contains no historical events, it cannot help date the book.
cultural:
The rose of Sharon and the lily of the valley (verse 1) were probably common wildflowers rather than the cultivated rose and lily of modern gardens; the first may have been a crocus or similar bloom, and the second possibly a lotus or lily. The woman may be modestly calling herself an ordinary flower of the field, and the man answers that she is a lily among thorns. The apple tree (verse 3) may be an apple, an apricot, or a quince; ancient identification is uncertain. Raisin cakes (verse 5) were a festive food, given out by David at the ark's arrival in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:19). Lovesickness, a longing so strong it makes one faint, is a common theme in ancient Egyptian love poetry as well.

The charge by the gazelles and does of the field (verse 7) is an oath formula, but instead of swearing by God it swears by graceful wild animals. Many scholars note that the Hebrew words for gazelles and does of the field sound like two titles of God, the LORD of Hosts and God Almighty, and suggest a deliberate play that avoids using God's name directly in a love poem. The little foxes of verse 15 were a real threat to vineyards, digging and eating the grapes, and the verse may picture any small danger that could spoil a budding love.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 7 continue the exchange of praise from chapter 1 and close the Song's first movement with the refrain: “Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.” Verses 8 to 17 open a new scene with the words Listen and Look, as the woman hears and then sees her beloved coming. His invitation (verses 10 to 13) is framed by the repeated call arise, come away, making it a small poem within the poem, a love song set in spring. Verse 14 pictures her as a dove hidden in the rocks, and verse 15 is a short, puzzling saying about foxes. Verse 16 is the first of the Song's three statements of mutual belonging (compare 6:3 and 7:10), and verse 17's call to be like a gazelle anticipates the Song's final verse (8:14).

outline.t: A lily among thorns, an apple tree among the trees
The house of wine and the lover's embrace
The charge: do not awaken love until the time is right
The beloved comes leaping over the hills
Arise, come away: the winter is past
The dove in the rock, and the little foxes
My beloved is mine and I am his

doctrines.note: “My beloved is mine and I am his” (2:16). The Song pictures love as mutual belonging, where each gives the self to the other. The charge not to awaken love before its time (2:7) adds that love must be guarded and ordered, not hurried.

The spring poem of verses 10 to 13 delights in the renewal of the created world: flowers, singing birds, ripening figs, and fragrant vines. The Song treats the beauty of nature and the beauty of love as belonging together, both gifts from the Maker.

words.note: Ahavah, love. It appears three times in the chapter, including the banner of love in verse 4, the lovesickness of verse 5, and the charge of verse 7. In the Song ahavah is not a feeling alone but a power, which can be stirred up or left sleeping, and which the book's climax will call as strong as death (8:6).

Ur, to rouse or awaken. It appears twice in verse 7: do not arouse or awaken love. The doubling makes the charge emphatic. Love is pictured as something that can be awakened too early, before the time is right. The same verb appears later in the Song (5:2; 8:5), and it gives the refrain its sense of caution and reverence before love's power.

Degel, banner or standard. In verse 4 his banner over me is love. A degel was a flag or sign that identified a group, especially the tribes of Israel in the wilderness camp (Numbers 2). The image may mean that love marks her as his, or that love is openly displayed like a military standard. Some scholars suggest a different meaning from a related word, his intention toward me is love, but banner is the common reading.

Shual, fox or jackal. The little foxes of verse 15 ruin the vineyards in bloom. The word covers both foxes and jackals, which damaged vineyards in ancient Israel. The saying may be a playful song or a serious warning, and many readers take it as a picture of small threats to love that must be dealt with before they cause harm.

christ: The New Testament never quotes this chapter. The connections Christians have drawn come through the wider Bible theme of God as the bridegroom of his people. Many hymns and devotional writings have taken up the phrase “his banner over me is love” as a picture of Christ's love covering the believer, and the invitation to arise and come away as the voice of Christ calling his people. Such readings belong to a long tradition of prayer and preaching, though they go beyond what the text itself claims. A reader who takes the chapter first as human love poetry can still see a reflection of the gospel in its central refrain. The mutual belonging of verse 16 echoes the covenant promise that runs through Scripture: I will be your God, and you will be my people (Jeremiah 30:22). In the New Testament that belonging is fulfilled in Christ, who gives himself for his bride, the church (Ephesians 5:25).

hard.q: What does the charge not to arouse or awaken love until the time is right mean?
hard.a: The refrain appears three times (2:7; 3:5; 8:4), each time after a scene of intimacy, and interpreters understand it in several ways. Many readers, Jewish and Christian, have taken it as a call to patience and chastity: love has great power, and its full expression should wait for the right time and setting, which the Song and the rest of Scripture locate in marriage. Others read it as a request not to disturb the lovers until their love has run its course, reading the Hebrew phrase as until it pleases rather than until the time is right. Still others see it as general wisdom about love's power: it should not be forced, manipulated, or stirred up artificially. These readings are not exclusive, and the refrain's placement after moments of closeness suggests that love's timing matters. The woman, who speaks the charge, is not ashamed of desire. She simply knows that it is strong enough to be handled with care.

questions: Why do you think the woman warns others not to awaken love until the time is right, even as she speaks so freely of her own love?
The spring poem celebrates new life after winter. What seasons of your life have felt like winter, and what did the arrival of spring look like?
What little foxes, small habits or irritations, can spoil a relationship if left unattended?
